messages.subject: Bayesian p-values
parts:
Hi all,


I am trying to calculate the Bayesian p-values for both a normal Cormack-Jolly-Seber (CJS) model and a spatial version of the CJS model (as described in the paper of Schaub and Royle, 2014). I would like to use Freeman-Tukey as a goodness of fit statistic instead of the Chi squared. Is it possible to calculate the Bayesian p-values when the data is not presented in an m-array and how can I implement the calculation of these p-values in the R scripts below?


Any help is appreciated!


Best regards,

Anne-Merel


MODEL 1:

sink("cjs-c-c.jags")

cat("

    model {

   

    # Priors and constraints

    for (i in 1:nind){

    for (t in f[i]:(n.occasions-1)){

    phi[i,t] <- mean.phi

    p[i,t] <- mean.p

    } #t

    } #i

   

    mean.phi ~ dunif(0, 1)         # Prior for mean survival

    mean.p ~ dunif(0, 1)           # Prior for mean recapture

   

    # Likelihood

    for (i in 1:nind){

    # Define latent state at first capture

    z[i,f[i]] <- 1

    for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){

    # State process

    z[i,t] ~ dbern(mu1[i,t])

    mu1[i,t] <- phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1]

    # Observation process

    y[i,t] ~ dbern(mu2[i,t])

    mu2[i,t] <- p[i,t-1] * z[i,t]

    } #t

    } #i

    ",fill = TRUE)

sink()

 

MODEL 2:

 

# Model sCJS-N

sink("sCJSN.mod")

cat("

    model {

 

    # Priors and constraints

    for (i in 1:nind){

    for (t in f[i]:(n.occasions-1)){

    phi[i,t] <- mean.phi

    p[i,t] <- mean.p

    } #t

    } #i

 

    mean.phi ~ dunif(0,1)

    mean.p ~ dunif(0,1)

    for (i in 1:2){

    tau[i] <- pow(sigma[i], -2)

    sigma[i] ~ dunif(0, 50)

    }

 

    # Likelihood

    for (i in 1:nind){

    # Define latent state at first capture

    z[i,f[i]] <- 1

    for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){

 

    # State processes

    # Survival

    z[i,t] ~ dbern(phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1])

    # Dispersal

    G[i,t,1] ~ dnorm(G[i,t-1,1], tau[1])

    G[i,t,2] ~ dnorm(G[i,t-1,2], tau[2])

 

    # Observation process

    # Test whether the actual location is in- or outside the state-space

    r[i,t] <- step(G[i,t,1]-Xmin) * step(Xmax-G[i,t,1]) * step(G[i,t,2]-Ymin) *

    step(Ymax-G[i,t,2])

    Y[i,t] ~ dbern(p[i,t-1] * z[i,t] * r[i,t])

    } #t

    } #i

    }

    ",fill = TRUE)

sink()

parts:
Dear Anne-Merel,

it is my understanding that this is not possible, because you cannot directly test the GoF for a model with binary response: you must aggregate the binary data first in some way. The m-array format is one such aggregation.

What's the reason for you not to run your analysis in the m-array format ? Do you have individual covariates ? If so, you could perhaps fit a similar model without them in the m-array format and do the GoF test there. You can then still work with your favourite model with these covariates, assuming that this latter model will fit better, since it explaines more variation.

Also, there are classical GoF tests for the CJS model that are informative about ways in which the assumptions of the model may be violated, e.g., by transients or trap-happiness. These are implemented in a program called RELEASE, which you can run through MARK (as far as I know). Regardless of whether you fit your model using Bayesian inference, these tests remain very interesting for an analysis.

Best regards  ---- Marc

parts:
Dear Anne-Merel,

capture-location is such an individual effect which you cannot fit in an analysis with the m-array aggregation (because individual identity is 'lost' in that aggregation). This may not be the best solution, but it seems like potentially useful to me to first ignore that covariate, do the m-array aggregation, fit a model and get a Bayesian p-value for a first, crude fit assessment. If you are lucky, this tells you that the model fits, so if you then do an analysis for the unaggregated data set, and with the location covariate added, then this model ought to fit be even better. If on the other hand the simpler model (without the location covariate) doesn't fit, then you may have to think about how to improve the model, e.g., by adding some random effects as a way to allow for 'overdispersion' or perhaps by adding effects for transients or trap-dependence (again, to diagnose the latter two, the tests in RELEASE can be valuable).

Best regards  ----  Marc

sink("cjs-c-c.jags")

cat("

    model {

   

    # Priors and constraints

    for (i in 1:nind){

    for (t in f[i]:(n.occasions-1)){

    phi[i,t] <- mean.phi

    p[i,t] <- mean.p

    } #t

    } #i

   

    mean.phi ~ dunif(0, 1)         # Prior for mean survival

    mean.p ~ dunif(0, 1)           # Prior for mean recapture

   

    # Likelihood

    for (i in 1:nind){

    # Define latent state at first capture

    z[i,f[i]] <- 1

    for (t in (f[i]+1):n.occasions){

    # State process

    z[i,t] ~ dbern(mu1[i,t])

    mu1[i,t] <- phi[i,t-1] * z[i,t-1]

    # Observation process

    y[i,t] ~ dbern(mu2[i,t])

    mu2[i,t] <- p[i,t-1] * z[i,t]

    } #t

    } #i

cat("

    model {

 

    # Priors and constraints

    for (i in 1:nind){

    for (t in f[i]:(n.occasions-1)){

    phi[i,t] <- mean.phi

    p[i,t] <- mean.p

    } #t

    } #i

 

    mean.phi ~ dunif(0,1)

    mean.p ~ dunif(0,1)

    for (i in 1:2){

    tau[i] <- pow(sigma[i], -2)

    sigma[i] ~ dunif(0, 50)

    }

    # Define latent state at first capture

Dear Anne-Merel,

capture-location is such an individual effect which you cannot fit in an analysis with the m-array aggregation (because individual identity is 'lost' in that aggregation). This may not be the best solution, but it seems like potentially useful to me to first ignore that covariate, do the m-array aggregation, fit a model and get a Bayesian p-value for a first, crude fit assessment. If you are lucky, this tells you that the model fits, so if you then do an analysis for the unaggregated data set, and with the location covariate added, then this model ought to fit be even better. If on the other hand the simpler model (without the location covariate) doesn't fit, then you may have to think about how to improve the model, e.g., by adding some random effects as a way to allow for 'overdispersion' or perhaps by adding effects for transients or trap-dependence (again, to diagnose the latter two, the tests in RELEASE can be valuable).

Hi Anne-Merel,

You can add groups to the dispersal process by adding an index to the location variance. We have an example in the Supplement to this paper: https://academic.oup.com/auk/article/135/1/29/5148574#supplementary-data

The model described there is pretty complex but you'll want to focus on the top of page 6, especially this:

 # Dispersal: the bird's current location is related to last year's location. Grouped by sex and last year's nest fate: 
 # Longitude: 
 G[i,t,1] ~ dnorm(G[i,t-1,1], tau_xy[1,sexes[i],nfates[i,t-1]]) 
 # Latitude: 
 G[i,t,2] ~ dnorm(G[i,t-1,2], tau_xy[2,sexes[i],nfates[i,t-1]])  

where sexes is a vector listing the sex (1 or 2) of each individual, and nfates is a matrix indicating the nest fate (1, 2, or 3) of each individual in each year.


I just noticed that the prior for tau_xy might have gotten left out of our supplemental code (sorry!). Here it is:

# priors for x and y variances (respectively); evaluated separately for each sex, nest fate:
for(i in 1:2){ # longitude and latitude
for(j in 1:nsx){ # sex
for(k in 1:nnf){ # nest fate
tau_xy[i,j,k] <- pow(sig_xy_sx_nf[i,j,k], -2)
sig_xy_sx_nf[i,j,k] ~ dunif(0,10)
}
}
}


Then in the initial values, the structure will always need to match what is in the model statement. For this model, I used:

sig_xy_sx_nf = array(runif(2*nsx*nnf,0.001,2),dim=c(2, nsx, nnf))

where nsx = number of sexes and nnf = number of nest fates being considered. Thus there is one initial value per latitude, longitude, sex, and nest fate.

Hope that helps,

Emily

Hi Anne-Merel,

You can add groups to the dispersal process by adding an index to the location variance. We have an example in the Supplement to this paper: https://academic.oup.com/auk/article/135/1/29/5148574#supplementary-data

The model described there is pretty complex but you'll want to focus on the top of page 6, especially this:

 # Dispersal: the bird's current location is related to last year's location. Grouped by sex and last year's nest fate: 
 # Longitude: 
 G[i,t,1] ~ dnorm(G[i,t-1,1], tau_xy[1,sexes[i],nfates[i,t-1]]) 
 # Latitude: 
 G[i,t,2] ~ dnorm(G[i,t-1,2], tau_xy[2,sexes[i],nfates[i,t-1]])  

where sexes is a vector listing the sex (1 or 2) of each individual, and nfates is a matrix indicating the nest fate (1, 2, or 3) of each individual in each year.


I just noticed that the prior for tau_xy might have gotten left out of our supplemental code (sorry!). Here it is:

# priors for x and y variances (respectively); evaluated separately for each sex, nest fate:
for(i in 1:2){ # longitude and latitude
for(j in 1:nsx){ # sex
for(k in 1:nnf){ # nest fate
tau_xy[i,j,k] <- pow(sig_xy_sx_nf[i,j,k], -2)
sig_xy_sx_nf[i,j,k] ~ dunif(0,10)
}
}
}


Then in the initial values, the structure will always need to match what is in the model statement. For this model, I used:

sig_xy_sx_nf = array(runif(2*nsx*nnf,0.001,2),dim=c(2, nsx, nnf))

where nsx = number of sexes and nnf = number of nest fates being considered. Thus there is one initial value per latitude, longitude, sex, and nest fate.

Hope that helps,

Emily
